cells.tense: You are in it now, curious and moving at the same time.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're learning and use it on the next step you actually take.
cells.core:
You're learning in the middle of moving, which is the rare version. Curiosity isn't slowing the pace down and the goal isn't killing the questions — the questions are being asked in the direction you're already facing. You find out what you need by going, not by waiting until you understand first.

What you find lands and it changes the next move, and the next move tells you what to go look for. That loop is doing the work. The easiest way to lose it is to hit a run of momentum and stop asking — so take the thing you're curious about and put it into the next concrete step, before the step is decided.
cells.sheetLine: You learn as you move, and the moving is better for it.

cells.tense: You're already living past the point where any of this gets settled.
cells.ask: Do the next physical step with what you have, without learning anything first.
cells.core:
You're studying the route instead of walking it. Every question opens two more and the goal keeps moving out ahead to wherever you'll be finished learning — and the momentum you were proud of is standing still under all that reading. It looks like progress, and it feels like it, and the distance isn't closing.

Some of this is real caution and worth keeping. But you can't think your way to the thing you'd learn by arriving, and the arrival keeps getting postponed until you're sure. Try the plain version: choose the next step you can take with what's already in your hands and move it today. Whatever you find on the other side of the doing will be different, and it'll be yours.

cells.tense: You are standing at a door you already went through, questions in hand.
cells.ask: Ask one plain question of something alive — a person, a page, a place — and follow the first answer.
cells.core:
The asking stopped. That's the plain fact of it. The direction is still there and the destinations haven't moved, but the questions don't come out anymore, and the way forward got narrower because of it.

This isn't solved by trying harder at it. It gets solved by being interested in something small and letting that pull — a person, a book, one actual question with an actual answer. Follow the answer wherever it goes for ten minutes, then notice what you have. What gets the line moving again is interest, not strain. Strain pushed at the quiet just makes the quiet louder.

cells.tense: You are already steering by things you know and calling it just going along.
cells.ask: Say one thing you've figured out as yours, out loud, then act on it.
cells.core:
There's more in your hands than your account of yourself admits, and it's already doing the steering. It shows in what you skip, what you choose without examining the choice, how you cut through a question straight to the answer. Yet it comes out sounding like the facts were doing the deciding and you were just following along.

This isn't modesty, or the work would be faster. It's a mislabeled author — you're reading the book and saying you didn't write it. Own one piece: name something you worked out and act on it without citing anything as the reason. Watch whether the thing you wanted to do changes once it's yours.
